items.title: Dick Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006
items.q: Remember, there was no Elvis at that time when we started and there was no rock & roll.

ctx.x: This is the music that they wanted, that they liked. Remember, there was no Elvis at that time when we started and there was no rock & roll. We were the kings. This is, you go to Eddie Condon’s or you go to Nick’s and that was the epitome of jazz and of popular music. It was the best. Hot music in its finest flower. And so we had no displeasure from the audience about playing that kind of music. We got great support from them. But of © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

course by the mid to late fifties rock & roll had come in and started to stifle a demand for Dixieland. We’re fortunate there are people as old as we around that liked it at Hamilton. And we’re also fortunate, I think Hamilton is, that the younger folks, the younger bands that play more modern music or folk music, are providing that for them. We don’t want to be the sole purveyor of music. It’s great that there is a choice now between audiences.
